newsitem.title: UK: Buyers again hold the reins in cash cocoa market.
newsitem.headline: Buyers again hold the reins in cash cocoa market.

text.p: Buyers are holding the reins in cash cocoa while Ivorian shippers continue to unfold long positions on the tailing main crop against a slim industry offtake, traders said on Wednesday.
A two-tier physical market is still in place and some sellers are offering cocoa at bargain differentials following a surge in the futures market.

"When you have a rally in the market you see some very low offers from shippers, you can have even 50 (stg) under LIFFE. They don't know anything about differentials. They just see the outright price and sell," said one.

The computer auction system in the Ivory Coast is often blamed for increased speculation by shippers who end up overbidding to secure cocoa from the Caisse and are then forced to hold back for market prices to catch up.
Some exporters who have dabbled the short side were having difficulty in getting hold of cocoa in time to meet the shipment deadline, traders said.
"It's difficult to talk about a differential market nowadays. We have to look at the outright levels from the origin," said one France-based trader.

Exports were down to a trickle -- one trader estimated daily offers of 2,000-3,000 tonnes on the current crop with sellers particularly keen to unwind longs to tap a favourable French franc/sterling exchange rate.
Ivorian differentials stood at 25-30 stg under the LIFFE May futures contract for nearby shipments to European destinations, traders said.

Industry buyers have disappeared after a flurry of purchases in the last two weeks following a surge in May cocoa to a seven-month peak of 1,048 stg a tonne. Big buyers are now mostly covered, some until November, but could be tempted to pick some more depending on the quality of the midcrop.

Industry cover increased recently after signs that Phibro, the trade house believed to control at least one third of world stocks, is eyeing long term gains and has no immediate plans to scale down its physical position.
But those demands (industry) were now met and there was little more buying left to be done, at least at current price levels, traders said.
